text:
A: Hello! Yes, I can see you. The happy lady with the books!
B: Ha! That's me, yeah. Hi, I'm Marta. Sorry, the books are a bit of a mess, I keep meaning to sort them out.
A: No, no, it looks good. My daughter Riya, she's eight, she wants a shelf like that. Hitesh, Peterborough. Where you're from? I hear little bit accent.
B: Yeah, Poland, Gdańsk, but I've lived in London fifteen years now. Walthamstow. What about you?
A: Gujarat, India. Came 2008, I married, wife's family was in Peterborough, so, Peterborough. What's your job?
B: I'm a pharmacist, in a hospital, on the heart wards. Erm, so I check everyone's medication and talk to patients before they go home.
A: Pharmacist! My wife, Komal, she works in pharmacy also. Counter, in the shop. She knows all the tablets, she tells me what to take, I don't listen.
B: Ha, that's what all my patients say about their wives. Does she enjoy it?
A: Yeah, she likes it. Full-time. She's the organised one, you know, bills, school forms, holidays, everything. Me, I'm the fun one.
B: Every house needs both, honestly. I'm the organised one in ours. I plan our holidays on spreadsheets, my husband just turns up at the airport.
A: Spreadsheet for holiday! No, mate. Too much. You just go.
B: I know, I know, but I like it, it's kind of half the fun for me. Where do you like to go?
A: India, mostly, weddings. Blackpool with the kids, London. And Dubai, my friend works there, I'm going this year. Definitely. Well, I say every year.
B: Oh, you should, though. Who books it, you or Komal?
A: Komal, obviously. Then I complain about flight time. Six in the morning, why, who flies six in the morning?
B: People who get the cheap flights! Sorry, that sounded like a spreadsheet person.
A: Ha! Yes, very spreadsheet. What you do, then, I'm in factory, flow-wrap machine, part-time. I do delivery also, moped, evenings. Good money, you know, if you know the right areas.
B: Oh, so you're working quite a lot of hours then, with both?
A: Er, depends. Part-time is my choice. Rules at the factory, mate, half of them pointless. Supervisor wants you standing there even when the machine is running perfectly.
B: I mean, we have loads of rules on the ward too, and some of them do feel a bit silly, but, erm, usually there's a story behind each one. Someone got hurt once, you know.
A: Maybe. Maybe. But some of them, no story, just somebody in an office. Anyway. Did you do the puzzle?
B: Badly. I gave up on the last one. Gurpreet, who I spoke to first, was much more patient than me.
A: Gurpreet, he looks like he knows his stuff. I just clicked anything. Uncle Abdul, he also, guessing. Nobody finished, I think.
B: That makes me feel better, honestly. So what do you do to relax, when you're not working?
A: Cricket. Watching, playing, Sunday in the park. And last night, Mumbai Indians, our guy drops simple catch, I'm still angry.
B: I don't really know cricket, to be honest, but my husband's English, so I've been made to watch some. It goes on for days, right?
A: Test, yes, five days, that's for old men. IPL is three hours, fast, everybody hitting sixes. Much better. You watch one with me, I explain, you'll love it.
B: Okay, deal, but you have to sit through a whole Polish volleyball match with—
